title: New US Immigration Rules in 2026: What H-1B, F-1 and Green Card Holders Must Know
excerpt: From the end of open-ended Duration of Status for F-1 students to a risky new advance parole ruling and steeper H-1B extension fees, 2026 has reshaped the landscape for Indian visa holders in America.
body:
• F-1 students will face a maximum four-year admission period starting September 15, ending the decades-old open-ended Duration of Status policy, with the post-study grace period cut from 60 to 30 days.
  • A Board of Immigration Appeals ruling dated August 13 makes travel on advance parole riskier — departures may now trigger 3-year or 10-year re-entry bans for those with unlawful presence history.
  • H-1B and L-1 visa extension petitions will cost employers an additional $4,000 and $4,500 respectively starting September 9, under the 9/11 response and biometric entry-exit fee.
  • USCIS officers now have expanded discretion to reject incomplete applications without issuing Requests for Evidence, effective August 5.

The year 2026 has delivered a wave of immigration policy changes that directly affect hundreds of thousands of Indian nationals living and working in the United States. From tighter student visa rules to new fees and a landmark advance parole decision, here is what visa holders need to know.

End of Open-Ended Duration of Status for F-1 Students

Starting September 15, 2026, the U.S. will impose a maximum four-year period of admission for F-1 students, ending the long-standing Duration of Status policy that allowed international students to remain for the length of their academic programs without a fixed end date. Students already in the country will need to request extensions beyond four years through a formal, paid application.

The post-completion grace period — the window to apply for Optional Practical Training, transfer programs, seek a change of status or exit the U.S. — has been halved from 60 days to 30 days. For Indian students, who make up the second-largest international student population in the U.S. with over 330,000 enrolled, the shorter timeline adds urgency to post-graduation planning.

Advance Parole Travel Now Riskier

A Board of Immigration Appeals decision dated August 13, 2026, has fundamentally changed the calculus for green card applicants who travel on advance parole. Under the new interpretation, departing the U.S. on advance parole is now treated as a departure that can trigger the 3-year or 10-year unlawful presence re-entry bar.

"Individuals with pending Adjustment of Status applications should not assume that an approved Advance Parole document makes international travel risk-free."

— Wildes & Weinberg, Immigration Law

The decision applies prospectively, meaning it does not retroactively affect those who previously traveled on advance parole. Immigration attorneys are advising anyone with a pending I-485 adjustment of status and any history of unlawful presence to consult an attorney before traveling internationally.

Higher Fees for H-1B and L-1 Extensions

Starting September 9, 2026, employers filing H-1B and L-1 visa extension petitions will pay additional fees under the 9/11 response and biometric entry-exit provision (Public Law 114-113). The surcharge adds $4,000 for H-1B renewals and $4,500 for L-1 extensions on top of regular USCIS filing fees. This applies to qualifying employers, typically those with 50 or more employees where more than half hold H-1B or L-1 status.

USCIS Tightens Rejection Standards

Effective August 5, 2026, USCIS officers have been granted expanded discretion to reject incomplete immigration applications outright, without issuing a Request for Evidence or Notice of Intent to Deny. Previously, applicants often received a second chance to submit missing documents within a 12-week window. The new policy applies to pending and newly filed applications, making thorough initial submissions essential.

New $1,000 Parole Fee Under HR-1

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act introduced a $1,000 fee for foreign nationals seeking entry under parole status. The fee applies at the time of entry unless one of 10 statutory exceptions applies. Adjustment of status applicants returning on advance parole after temporary travel abroad are generally exempt, but immigration lawyers advise documenting that exemption carefully.

Other Changes Taking Effect

Several additional rules round out the 2026 immigration overhaul. Minor visa applicants of all ages must now appear in person for consular interviews at U.S. embassies, including infants. U.S. Customs and Border Protection has rolled out a 10-day email alert system warning B1/B2 visitors about their remaining authorized stay, with plans to expand to F, J, H-1B and H-2 categories. And the Trump administration's stricter public charge rule, effective September 18, will allow USCIS officers to deny green cards to applicants deemed likely to depend on government benefits like food stamps, Medicaid and housing vouchers.

Updated USCIS forms I-539 and I-765 take effect September 15, with no grace period for outdated editions.
